analysis.one_liner: Forces brand-name drug makers to sell samples of their drugs to companies developing cheaper generic and biosimilar versions.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with one Republican sponsor, one Democratic sponsor, and 13 cosponsors to stop brand-name drug makers from blocking generic competition died in a House committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: To develop a generic drug, a company must test its copy against the brand-name original. Brand-name makers sometimes refuse to sell samples of their drugs, or use safety programs as a cover to withhold them, which delays cheaper competition. This bill would require license holders to supply testing samples within 30 days at market-based prices, give FDA a process to authorize access to tightly restricted drugs, and let companies that are refused sue for damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would pay less as generics and biosimilars reach the market sooner, and the smaller companies that make them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits a drug's license holder from applying any sale or distribution restriction, including safety-program restrictions, in a way that cuts off the supply of samples to a company developing a generic or biosimilar.
For drugs not under restricted distribution, the license holder must provide the requested quantity within 30 days at a market-based price it has charged others.
For drugs under restricted safety programs (REMS), FDA can authorize a developer to obtain the product, and the license holder must then supply it through a designated wholesaler within 30 days.
A developer that is refused can sue for injunctions and treble damages, and wholesalers cannot tell the brand-name maker who requested samples.
Congress's own findings state that these access restrictions deter and delay generics and biosimilars, extending monopolies beyond their lawful patent life.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, who lose a tool for slowing generic competition and may see cheaper copies reach the market years earlier.

drawbacks.text: The bill shields brand-name makers from liability for anything that goes wrong during a developer's testing, which shifts safety risk onto the testing companies.

The bill creates a private right of action with treble damages on top of FDA's existing enforcement authority, which critics could call duplicative litigation pressure; and for tightly restricted drugs, safety protections depend on FDA's case-by-case judgment that a developer's protocol is comparable to the brand's safeguards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster generic and biosimilar competition, which historically drives large price reductions for patients. The bill contains real safeguards: FDA must approve access to the most dangerous restricted drugs, it retains power to block transfers posing a public health hazard, and testing companies bear liability for their own conduct. The main cost falls on brand-name makers' delayed-exclusivity strategies, not on patient safety.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley (R-WV) introduced the FAST Generics Act on April 6, 2017, joined by Rep. Peter Welch (D-VT), and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever taken on it.
Thirteen members cosponsored the bill, 9 Democrats and 4 Republicans, giving it bipartisan support before it stalled.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill never received a committee vote or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, which kept the ability to restrict access to samples and continued delaying cheaper generic and biosimilar competition.

for.name: Rep. David McKinley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed requiring drug makers to supply testing samples to generic and biosimilar developers.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Democratic co-lead.

for.name: 13 cosponsors (9 Democrats, 4 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the entire 115th Congress.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Drug license holders whose distribution restrictions the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: The bill's own findings describe license holders restricting competitive access to their products; the industry generally opposed requirements to surrender samples that slow generic entry.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican lead sponsor and 9 Democratic cosponsors out of 13 — but the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would strip them of the ability to withhold samples or misuse safety programs to delay generics and biosimilars, ending a tactic that extends monopolies beyond their patent life at patients' expense.
The bill guarantees them access to testing samples at market prices and a right to sue if refused, letting cheaper products reach the market sooner.
They would become the designated channel for sample requests and gain that business, but must keep the requesting developer's identity confidential.
